main.text: In the writings of the Prophets there occur three histories or prophecies about locusts that are remarkable above the rest, and which must therefore be explained here. The first concerns the Egyptian locusts, that is, those sent by God into Egypt after the seven most dreadful plagues, by which the obstinacy of Pharaoh could not be broken [Exod. X, 4. ff.]. In this [col. 461] history, in order to understand what is said about the locusts, these three things must be observed. 1. In general, how great a destruction locusts cause to herbs, crops, trees and every produce of the earth. 2. What was peculiar in these locusts. 3. How they were brought into Egypt and carried away out of Egypt. On the first point we would labour in vain if locusts were as well known to us as to the Arabs and Africans, who learn daily how grievous this evil is. When the harvests are already ripe, or upon meadows and pastures, or upon gardens and orchards, a thousand myriads of locusts descend, which, consuming the labour of a whole year in a few hours, impose famine upon the wretched inhabitants. This voracity and gluttony the Arabs express by the words احتنك [iḥtanaka] to gulp down (a word derived from حنك [ḥanak], that is, the jaws); نعص [naʿaṣa] or لعص [laʿaṣa], to devour (Lam and Nun being interchanged); دبش [dabasha], to strip the bark (which, however, they take of the earth and the fields, not of trees, as if the crops and herbs that the locusts consume were the bark of the earth); بشر [bashara], to scrape like a hide, and to make smooth: جرد [jarada], to make bare and to strip of hair: whence also the very name of the locust, جراد [jarād]. Indeed these little creatures gulp down, devour, strip, scrape and make bare whatever is green in the fields. Nor do they harm by their bite alone; they also scorch by their touch. Moreover لعابهم سم ناقع للنبات والشجر لا يقع علي شي منه الا اهلكه [luʿābuhum samm nāqiʿ li-l-nabāt wa-l-shajar lā yaqaʿu ʿalā shayʾ minhu illā ahlakahu] their saliva is a poison so harmful to herbs and trees that whatever it falls upon, it destroys; as one may read in Damir. Yet these things may seem slight, since they often inflict much more damage dead than alive, infecting the air with a foul and poisonous stench, from which a most severe pestilence follows, so that more myriads of men are carried off by such a plague in a few days than by long wars; as will be said in its place. Hence the same Damir says: ليس في الحيوان اكثر افسان [laysa fī al-ḥayawān akthar afsān] There is no animal more destructive. And Muhammad, as they say: الله خلق الف امة منها ستماية في البحر واربعماية في البر وان اول هلاك هذه الامم الجراد واذا اهلك الجراد تتابع هلاك الامم كنظم السلك [Allāh khalaqa alf umma minhā sittumiʾa fī al-baḥr wa-arbaʿumiʾa fī al-barr wa-inna awwal halāk hādhihi al-umam al-jarād wa-idhā halaka al-jarād tatābaʿa halāk al-umam ka-naẓm al-silk] God created a thousand species of animals, [III, 283] six hundred in the sea and four hundred on land. But the first plague of these is the locust; when it destroys, the ruin of the rest follows, like a strung necklace: that is, as the beads strung on a necklace follow one another ^{(1)}.

[III, 284] But in the Egyptian locusts there was something more grievous than usual. For although no plague is more frequent in Egypt, Moses nevertheless says expressly ^{a)} that there had never been locusts like these, nor would there be in the future; whether because they were larger in bulk, like those Indian locusts which Pliny writes, book 9, ch. 3, fill four cubits, and book 10, ch. 29, are three feet in length, their legs and thighs serving as saws when they have dried out; or, as I rather believe, because they surpassed in number whatever swarm of locusts had ever been anywhere in one place, and were more harmful. This is suggested by the words of the Prophet: that they so covered the surface of the earth [col. 462] that no one could see the ground; and that they settled over the whole land of Egypt, whereas locusts usually fly into this or that field, passing over others; and that they consumed every herb, and all the fruit of the trees, and whatever the hail that had gone before had left.

If at these words you ask what this remainder was, since we read that the hail struck whatever was in the fields in all the land of Egypt, and damaged every herb, and broke every tree, Exod. IX, 25.? I answer: 1. The wheat and the spelt were not damaged by the hail. For so the sacred text has it in verses 31 and 32: But the flax and the barley were damaged, because the barley had its stalk, and the flax its stem. But the wheat and the spelt were not damaged, because they were late. For in those places wheat comes up later than barley. Hence Clement of Alexandria, book 6 of the Stromata, [III, 285] Προπετεστέρα εἰς ὥραν θέρους τοῦ πυροῦ, μᾶλλον ἡ κριθή [propetestera eis hōran therous tou pyrou, mallon hē krithē]: Barley comes sooner than wheat in the summer season. And Pliny, book 18, ch. 17: In Egypt barley is reaped in the sixth month from sowing, wheat in the seventh: that is, one month later ^{(2)}. Hence, compared with barley, they are called אפילות, that is, late. Not because they were still entirely hidden under the earth, as Junius and Tremellius render it following Kimchi; for they had long since come up. Rather, being still tender, by their pliant and flexible softness they avoided and escaped the blows of the falling hail, as is rightly observed by Fuller, Miscellanea book 3, ch. 11. Further, it is likely that, like the wheat and the spelt, certain herbs and grasses, and also the branches and fruits of some trees, escaped the force of the hail. Thus it is not without hyperbole that the hail is said to have damaged every herb and every tree. The exception that follows plainly shows this. Or it must be said that it damaged all herbs and trees in such a way that it did not destroy them entirely.

Most, in order to untie this knot, imagine that many months, or even a year, passed between the plague of hail and the plague of locusts, and that in the meantime new grass, new crops and new fruits of the trees grew in place of those that the hail had destroyed. This seems to be said in vain, since Moses writes expressly that the locusts consumed whatever the hail had left remaining, Exod. X, 5. 12. 15. Nor could the hail be said to have left remaining what did not yet exist, or did not yet stand above the ground. Moreover, from the time when Moses began to perform miracles in Egypt until his death, exactly forty years passed. For he was in his eightieth year when he met Pharaoh, Exod. VII, 7. And in the hundred and twentieth year of his age he died on the border of the land of Canaan, which he had seen from Mount Nebo, Deut. XXXIV, 1. 5. Through these forty years, further, the Israelites are said to have journeyed through the desert, Ios. V, 6. This could not stand if Moses had spent a whole year in Egypt performing miracles. For that year would have to be subtracted from the forty years of the Israelites' stay in the desert. It is therefore false, as these suppose, that a long interval passed between the miracles of Moses. Nor does it accord well with the goodness of God that, when his people had already been reduced to extremity, he should have come to their aid so slowly and with so many delays. And his justice too required that he punish so grave a σκληροκαρδίαν [sklērokardian] of Pharaoh with continuous plagues, granting him no breathing space. We therefore side with those who compress the ten plagues inflicted on the Egyptians into a short time, say a month or thereabouts.

[III, 286] A point I had nearly omitted: these locusts filled not only the fields but also the houses of the Egyptians, Exod. X, 6. ^{(3)}. And they are thought to have been harmful not only to the fruits of the earth and of the trees, but also to men; and to this, it is thought, refers what is said of the enemies of the church, Sap. XVI, 9. Οὓς μὲν γὰρ ἀκρίδων καὶ μυιῶν ἀπέκτεινε δήγματα, καὶ οὐχ εὑρέθη ἴαμα τῇ ψυχῇ αὐτῶν, ὅτι ἄξιοι ἦσαν ὑπὸ τοιούτων κολασθῆναι [Hous men gar akridōn kai myiōn apekteine dēgmata, kai ouch heurethē iama tē psychē autōn, hoti axioi ēsan hypo toioutōn kolasthēnai]. For the bites of locusts and flies killed them, and no remedy was found for their soul [col. 463] (that is, their life), because they deserved to be punished by such things. But the author of the book seems to rely on the words with which Pharaoh asked to be freed from this plague, Exod. X, 17. Entreat the Lord your God, that he take away from me this death. Yet from this it by no means follows that these locusts inflicted death on men. For there is also a death of fields, of herbs and of trees. So the Egyptians say, Gen. XLVII, 19. Why should we die before you, both we and our land? And of a tree, Job XIV, 8. If its root grow old in the earth, and its stock die in the dust. And David, Psal. LXXVIII, 47: He killed their vines with hail. And Paul, 1 Cor. XV, 36: What you sow is not quickened unless it first dies. On this expression more is said at the very beginning of this work ^{(4)}. Moreover, locusts kill men and beasts at least by consequence, [III, 287] as they say, since by consuming what would have served to sustain life they thus drive them to death ^{(5)}. In either respect, therefore, Pharaoh could ask that God take away this death, that is, these deadly locusts.

Moreover, just as these locusts had been brought into Egypt by the קדים Kadim wind, that is, the east wind, so they were carried away by the ים wind, the wind of the sea, that is, the west wind, and cast into the Red Sea. For that locusts are carried by the wind is commonplace. Pliny, in the place cited above: "There is also another way in which they perish. Lifted up in swarms by the wind, they fall into seas or pools." Jerome on Joel ch. 2: "In our own times too we have seen swarms of locusts cover the land of Judaea: which afterwards, by the mercy of the Lord, etc., when a wind arose, were hurled into the first and the last sea." Orosius, book 4, ch. 11, on the African locusts: "Seized by a sudden wind, and driven together into masses, and carried for a long time through the air, they were plunged into the African sea" ^{(6)}. But the קדים Kadim wind, which brought the locusts into Egypt, although properly it means the east wind, is nevertheless also taken for the south wind, as we proved ^{b)} in the chapter On the Miracle of the Quails. Thus the Greek translators render it Νότον [Noton] and Λίβα [Liba], that is, Notus and Africus, and καύσωνα [kausōna], the burning wind. And perhaps it will not be beside the point to interpret it so here: since the east wind could have brought locusts into Egypt only from Arabia, but the south wind from Ethiopia, which is far more fertile in this pest. Accordingly الحبشان [al-ḥbshān] alhabsan, a kind of locust, takes its name [III, 288] from the Abaseni, or Abyssinians, in whose soil it is born. And in Ethiopia some peoples lived on locusts alone, which the winds, partly westerly, partly southerly, carried there in an almost incredible abundance. And this around the spring equinox, the very time of year at which they were brought into Egypt. Agatharchides, where he speaks of the Acridophagi: Ὑπὸ δὲ τὴν ἐαρινὴν ἰσημερίαν, ὅτε Λίβες παρ᾽ αὐτοῖς καὶ Ζέφυροι πνέουσι παμμεγέθεις, ἀκρίδων πλῆθος ἀμύθητον ἐκ τῆς ἀνιστορήτου μετὰ τῶν ἀνέμων παραγίνεται χώρας [Hypo de tēn earinēn isēmerian, hote Libes par᾽ autois kai Zephyroi pneousi pammegetheis, akridōn plēthos amythēton ek tēs anistorētou meta tōn anemōn paraginetai chōras]. And Diodorus, book 3: Κατὰ γὰρ τὴν ἐαρινὴν ὥραν παρ᾽ αὐτοῖς Ζέφυροι καὶ Λίβες παμμεγέθεις ἐκρίπτουσιν ἐκ τῆς ἐρήμου πλῆθος ἀκρίδων ἀμύθητον [Kata gar tēn earinēn hōran par᾽ autois Zephyroi kai Libes pammegetheis ekriptousin ek tēs erēmou plēthos akridōn amythēton]. And Strabo, book 16: Ζῶσι δ᾽ ἀπὸ ἀκρίδων, ἃς οἱ ἐαρινοὶ Λίβες, καὶ Ζέφυροι, πνέοντες μεγάλοι, συνελαύνουσιν εἰς τοὺς τόπους τούτους [Zōsi d᾽ apo akridōn, has hoi earinoi Libes, kai Zephyroi, pneontes megaloi, synelaunousin eis tous topous toutous]. Accordingly these same winds seem to have brought the locusts into Egypt from the same places, that is, from Ethiopia ^{(7)}. For as to the view of most, that they were created by God, they will hardly persuade me of it; because Scripture relates nothing of the kind, but says that they were brought by a wind which blew all day and all night. Nor are miracles to be invented without necessity. None such appears here, since more locusts are produced in Ethiopia, near Egypt, than in any part of the world. The miracle, therefore, lay not in God's producing so prodigious a multitude of locusts, but in his bringing it at his nod. And in that the same God who had brought them, at the prayer of Moses, his servant, [col. 464] immediately took them away, raising another wind, namely the west wind, which the Hebrews call רוח ים, the wind of the sea, because they have the sea to the west. And as that wind blew with great force, all the locusts were cast into the Red Sea, not even one being left in all the borders of Egypt. For since the Red Sea lies to the east of Egypt, they had to be driven there by a west wind.

notes.text: How much damage swarms of locusts inflict on the regions of Syria and Egypt will be better understood from what the writers both of histories and of travels report to us. GREGORIUS BARHEBRAEUS, also called ABULPHARAGIUS, in his Chronicle, written in Syriac, copied by Bruns from a Bodleian manuscript and edited by Kirsch, p. 134: ܒܫܢܬ ܐܨܗ ܕܝ̈ܘܢܝܐ ܐܬܐ ܩܡܨܐ ܦܪܚܐ ܘܚܒܠ ܙܪ̈ܥܐ ܘܐܪܡܝ ܙܪܥܐ ܘܢܦܩ. ܘܡܣܒܟ ܗܘܐ ܘܣܠܩ ܒܫܘܪ̈ܐ ܘܐܣ̈ܐ. ܘܥܐܠ ܡܢ ܟܘ̈ܐ ܘܬܪ̈ܥܐ ܠܒ̈ܬܐ. ܘܐܬܡܠܝܘ ܡܢܗ ܐܦ ܓܪ̈ܒܐ ܕܡ̈ܝܐ ܘܬܫܘܝ̈ܬܐ ܘܦܬܘܪ̈ܐ ܘܠܓ̈ܐ. ܘܟܕ ܡܢ ܦܢܝܬ ܬܝܡܢܐ ܥܐܠ ܗܘܐ ܠܒܝܬܐ ܡܢ ܓܒܐ ܓܪܒܝܝܐ ܢܦܩ ܗܘܐ. ܘܐܟܠ ܥܡ ܥܣܒܐ ܘܐܝܠ̈ܢܐ. ܐܦ ܡܐ̈ܢܐ ܕܥܡܪܐ ܘܢܚ̈ܬܐ ܕܒ̈ܢܝܢܫܐ. ܘܟܕ ܓܡܪ ܠܟܠܗ ܦܢܝܬܐ ܕܐܘܪܗܝ ܘܣܪܘܓ ܥܒܪ ܠܡܥܪܒܐ. In the year of the Greeks 1095 (which was 784 after Christ) flying locusts burst in, spoiled the crops and laid eggs; and those hatched from them, after they had grown wings, climbed the walls and partitions, and entered the houses through the windows and doors [cf. Exod. X, 6. ומלאו בתיך ובתי כל עבדיך ובתי כל מצרים, They shall fill (the locusts) your houses, and those of your courtiers and of your subjects]. The water jars, the floors, the tables and the dishes were filled with them. After they had entered the houses from the southern side, they went out on the northern side, having consumed the plants, the trees, even the woollen garments and the clothing of men. When the whole region of Edessa and Sarug had been laid waste, they passed on towards the west. And the continuator of Barhebraeus, in dem Neuen Repertorio für bibl. und morgenl. Literat. edited by Paulus, vol. 1, p. 67 f. [the Syriac, 10 lines, not transcribed here]: In the year 1774 (1463 after Christ) many locusts came from the east, and wingless ones at that [so, it seems, the words ܘܕܒܒܐ ܐܝܬܝܗܘܢ ܗܘܐ should be rendered, which Bruns translated: and flies burst in. But ܕܒܒܐ here undoubtedly agrees in meaning with the Arabic دُبَّاءٌ [dubbāʾ], a locust not yet winged]. They came as far as Egypt, ate the crops, vineyards, fruits, trees, even the grass, and left nothing green on the face of the earth. The vineyards, fruits and trees failed, gnawed bare and devoured by the locusts. LEO AFRICANUS in the Descript. Africae [III, 284] book 2, ch. 11, p. 77, Zurich edition 1559: When I was staying among them (the people of Tagtessa), a great multitude of locusts had invaded that region; I would dare to affirm that they had grown so large that they far exceeded the ears of grain, which had then reached ripeness, so that the very surface of the ground was completely covered with locusts. [Cf. Exod. X, 15. ויכס את עין כל הארץ ותחשך הארץ They covered the whole surface of the earth and darkened it.] And this was in the year 919, which was 1510 of Christ. The same Leo, book 9, ch. 61, p. 512: In Africa locusts are generally seen in such numbers that in flight they cover the rays of the sun like a cloud. They eat the very trees together with their leaves and fruit. When about to depart they leave eggs, from which others spring up (although these do not fly), and wherever they are met with they eat everything down to the bark of the trees, and leave behind a great dearth of grain, especially in Mauritania. LE BRUN, Voyages au Levant p. 252, mentions a swarm of locusts that had consumed everything green within the space of two hours, and the places in Cyprus through which these insects had passed were as though laid waste by fire. Russell relates the same in the Natural History of Aleppo p. 62 (Of the noxious kind may well be reckoned the locust, which sometimes arrive in such incredible multitudes, that it would appear fabulous to relate, destroying the whole of the verdure where-ever they pass). Whoever wants more should consult OEDMANN in den Vermischten Sammlungen, fasc. 2, ch. 6, p. 95 ff., and our Scholia on Exod. X, 14. p. 450 ff., second edition.
In Egypt barley ripens in the month of February; wheat lasts until the end of March, says Forsskål in the Prolegomenn. ad Flor. Aegypt. p. 43.
Compare the passage of Barhebraeus quoted above, note 1.

Vol. I, book 1, Chapter 1, p. 1. I shall add the words that bear on this: "Just as an animal is called ζῶον [zōon] in Greek, so in Hebrew it is called חיה by reason of life. Not that in the view of the Hebrews life is proper to the animal, as the learned think. For Aben Ezra and Ramban, on the first chapter of Genesis, acknowledge that there is life in plants. And this is clear from Scripture, when it promises that men shall live like grain, Os. XIV, 7. To which the Apostle alludes, 1 Cor. XV, 36. Accordingly trees are said to be killed and to die, that is, to be deprived of life. Thus Ps. LXXVIII, 47: He killed their vines with hail. On these words Kimchi says: גם יתכן בצומח מיתה אחר אשר בו נפש הצומחת, Death also befits a plant, since there is a vegetative soul in it. Hence Horace, book 1, Epist. 12: But whether you slaughter fish, or leek and onion. And Seneca, Epist. 58: For it is held that crops and shrubs have a soul: and so we say that they both live and die. To the same point are these words of Job about a tree, ch. 14, v. 8: Though its root grow old in the earth, and its stock die in the dust. And the outcry of the Egyptians to Joseph, Genes. XLVII, 19: Why should we die before you, both we and our land? For the land is said to die when it lies uncultivated and desolate, since it lives in some way in its produce. Hence Martial, book 13, Epigr. 12: — — lest the suburban field should die. And Statius, book 5 of the Thebaid, on the serpent by which Archemorus was killed: — the grass, struck by its hot breath, falls where it bore its jaws; the field dies at its hissing. Therefore that the plant lives is admitted among the Hebrews too. But because the animal alone feels, desires and moves, life is sometimes attributed to it as its own, since it rises many degrees above the life of the plant."

The carcasses of locusts also infect the air with stench and noxious exhalations, so that evil diseases arise. JEROME, in his Commentary on Joel, Chapter 2, on the swarms of locusts that infested Palestine in his time: When the shores of both seas were filled with heaps of dead locusts, which the waters had cast up, their putrefaction and stench was so harmful that it corrupted the air as well, and a pestilence arose among beasts as well as men. ATHANAS. KIRCHER, in Scrutinium physico-medicum contagiosae luis, Leipzig 1659, p. 43: There can be no plainer sign of an epidemic sickness soon to follow than swarms of locusts flying through the summer. FRID. HOFFMANN, in Medicina Systematica, T. II, vol. II, ch. 4, §. 14: In the year 1692 an incredible quantity of locusts was seen flying in the air, which infested all Thuringia, Meissen and the Vogtland, and, descending to the ground, did very great damage to the crops and vegetation; from which time many malignant fevers, indeed fevers joined with petechiae, began to rage in these regions. IGNAC. DE ASSO confirms this very thing with several testimonies in the book often cited, Chapter 2, p. 12–15, German trans.

THEVENOT, Travels, vol. I, p. 12: Heavy rains kill the locusts. — The Cossacks are freed from locusts only in this way, unless perhaps, after they have begun to fly, the north wind or the Corus carries them off into the Black Sea. HASSELQUIST himself saw at Smyrna great swarms of locusts hurled into the sea by the wind, Itin. p. 253. 254.

Nothing, however, prevents us from understanding the east wind in this passage, since Arabia, because of its deserts and its sandy and barren hills, especially favours the breeding of locusts (Cf. OEDMANN, Histor. Nat. Arabiae petraeae, in his Vermischte Sammlungen, Fasc. 6, ch. 24, p. 176), and even now many swarms of them are often carried from Arabia both into Eretz Yisrael and Syria and into Egypt.
